entry:
Modern form of the metric system and the world's most widely used system of measurement, abbreviated SI (from French *Système international d'unités*). It is the only system with official status in nearly every country and is used in science, technology, industry, and commerce. The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) coordinates it.

The SI comprises seven base units: the [[Second]] (s, time), [[Metre]] (m, length), [[Kilogram]] (kg, mass), [[Ampere]] (A, electric current), [[Kelvin]] (K, thermodynamic temperature), [[Mole (unit)|mole]] (mol, amount of substance), and [[Candela]] (cd, luminous intensity). Twenty-two coherent derived units, always expressible as products of powers of the base units, have special names and symbols, and 24 prefixes, such as kilo- for 10³ and nano- for 10⁻⁹, produce decimal multiples and sub-multiples.

The base units are defined through seven defining constants with exact values: the speed of light, the hyperfine transition frequency of caesium, the Planck constant, the elementary charge, the Boltzmann constant, the Avogadro constant, and the luminous efficacy Kcd. The kilogram, for example, rests on the Planck constant h being 6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J⋅s. A revision adopted by the 26th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in 2018, effective May 20, 2019, redefined the kilogram, ampere, kelvin, and mole this way, completing a move away from physical artifacts, which can be lost, damaged, or changed.

The system arose from the diversity of units in the centimetre–gram–second (CGS) systems and a lack of coordination among disciplines. The CGPM, established by the Metre Convention of 1875, set the definitions and rules. An initiative begun in 1948 led to publication of the system in 1960.

Global system of interconnected computer networks using the [[Internet protocol suite]] (TCP/IP) to communicate between networks and devices. A network of networks, it links private, public, academic, business, and government networks by electronic, wireless, and optical technologies.

The internet carries services such as the hypertext documents of the [[World Wide Web]], [[Email|electronic mail]], internet telephony, streaming media, and file sharing. It has transformed telephone, radio, television, paper mail, and newspapers, and has enabled instant messaging, social networking, and online shopping. The web is only one of many internet services. About 5.5 billion people, 68% of the world's population, used the internet by 2024, with use correlating strongly with economic development.

Its origins lie in time-sharing of computer resources, packet switching, and computer networks. Paul Baran at RAND in the early 1960s and, independently, Donald Davies at the United Kingdom's National Physical Laboratory in 1965 pioneered packet switching. The [[ARPANET]], proposed by the Advanced Research Projects Agency of the [[United States Department of Defense]], first linked two nodes, at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] and the Stanford Research Institute, on October 29, 1969. By the end of 1971, 15 sites were connected. Protocols for internetworking came from research commissioned in the 1970s by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) with universities and researchers in the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. The NSFNET backbone in the 1980s and privatization in the 1990s turned a research network into commercial infrastructure.

The internet has no single centralized governance, and each constituent network sets its own policies. The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) directs the [[IP address]] space and the Domain Name System, while the non-profit Internet Engineering Task Force standardizes the core protocols.

Country in West Asia (pop. over 92 million), officially the Islamic Republic of Iran and historically known as Persia. Its capital and largest city is [[Tehran]]. Iran borders Iraq, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan, and Pakistan, with the Caspian Sea to the north and the Gulf of Oman and the [[Persian Gulf]] to the south. It covers 1,648,195 sq km and is divided into 31 provinces.

Iran is home to one of the world's oldest continuous major civilizations. The territory was first unified under the Medes in the 7th century BC and reached its height in the 6th century BC, when [[Cyrus the Great]] founded the [[Achaemenid Empire]]. Alexander the Great conquered the empire in the 4th century BC. The Parthian Empire arose in the 3rd century BC and was succeeded in the 3rd century AD by the Sasanian Empire. Islamization followed the 7th-century Muslim conquest. In the 16th century the [[Safavid dynasty]] re-established a unified state with Twelver Shia Islam as the official religion. The Pahlavi dynasty was founded in 1925 by Reza Shah, and attempts by Mohammad Mosaddegh to nationalize the oil industry led to the Anglo-American coup in 1953.

The [[Iranian Revolution]] of 1979 overthrew the monarchy, and [[Ruhollah Khomeini]] became the first supreme leader of the Islamic Republic. Iraq invaded in 1980, beginning the eight-year [[Iran–Iraq War]].

Iran is a theocratic Islamic republic in which ultimate authority rests with the supreme leader; key offices, including head of state and the military, are not subject to public vote. The government has been widely criticized internationally for restrictions on assembly, expression, and the press and for its treatment of women, ethnic minorities, and dissidents. The economy is centrally planned with significant state ownership, and large fossil fuel reserves make Iran a regional power. Its nuclear program is among the most scrutinized in the world. Iran has 30 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Israeli strikes in 2025 escalated into the Twelve-Day War. In 2026 the United States and Israel launched a war with Iran in which supreme leader Ali Khamenei was killed; his son Mojtaba Khamenei succeeded him.

Final epoch of the three-age system of technology, following the Copper Age and the [[Bronze Age]], defined by smelted iron, especially steel tools and weapons, replacing bronze equivalents in common use. The concept originated in describing Europe and the ancient Near East. Its start is fixed locally by archaeological convention, and the notion is being challenged.

In [[Anatolia]] and the Caucasus, or Southeast Europe, the Iron Age began c. 1300 BC. In the ancient Near East it coincided with the [[Late Bronze Age collapse]] in the 12th century BC. The technology spread through the Mediterranean basin and to South Asia between the 12th and 11th centuries BC, and reached Northern Europe only c. the 5th century BC. In India the period runs from the ironworking Painted Grey Ware culture, c. 1200 BC, to the reign of Ashoka in the 3rd century BC. Many parts of Africa passed directly from stone to iron, and some archaeologists believe iron metallurgy developed independently in sub-Saharan Africa as early as 2000 BC. The term is rarely used for China, where written history began before iron smelting.

Meteoric iron, a natural iron–nickel alloy, was used thousands of years earlier; the oldest known artifacts are nine small beads dated to 3200 BC from burials at Gerzeh in Lower Egypt. An Iron Age culture is marked by mass production of tools and weapons from smelted steel alloys with added carbon, which are harder and lighter than bronze. Smelting iron requires temperatures above 1,250 °C, impractical for most of the Bronze Age, whereas copper melts at 1,085 °C and tin at 231.9 °C. The earliest tentative evidence of iron-making is a few steel-like fragments from Kaman-Kalehöyük in Turkey, dated to 2200–2000 BC.

End dates vary: c. 550 BC with the Persian [[Achaemenid Empire]] in the Near East, the 1st century BC with Roman conquest in Central and Western Europe, and c. AD 800 with the Viking Age in Scandinavia. Christian Jürgensen Thomsen introduced the three-age system to Scandinavia in the 1830s.

Chemical element, symbol Fe (from Latin *ferrum*), atomic number 26, a transition metal in group 8 of the [[Periodic table|periodic table]]. By mass it is the most common element on Earth, forming much of the core, and the fourth most abundant in the [[Earth's crust]]. Pure iron is a lustrous, ductile, silvery metal with a melting point of 1538 °C, a boiling point of 2861 °C, and a density of 7.87 g/cm³.

Iron's metallic form was long supplied mainly by meteorites. Extracting usable metal from ores such as [[Hematite|hematite]] and [[Magnetite|magnetite]] requires furnaces reaching 1,500 °C, about 500 °C hotter than for copper. Humans mastered this in Eurasia during the 2nd millennium BC, and the displacement of copper alloys by iron tools and weapons marks the start of the [[Iron Age]]. Iron alloys, above all [[Steel|steel]], are by far the most common industrial metals because of their mechanical properties and low cost; nearly 98% of mined iron ore goes into steel production.

Solid iron has several crystal forms. Molten iron freezes at 1538 °C into body-centered cubic δ-iron, changes to face-centered cubic γ-iron at 1394 °C, and returns to body-centered cubic α-iron at 912 °C and below. At high pressures it adopts the hexagonal ε form, presumed to make up the Earth's inner core as an iron–nickel alloy. Below its Curie point of 770 °C, α-iron is ferromagnetic.

Iron reacts with oxygen and water to form brown-to-black hydrated oxides known as [[Rust|rust]]. Because rust occupies more volume than the metal and flakes off, it exposes fresh surface to corrosion. The most common oxidation states are +2 and +3, but compounds range from −2 to +7.

Iron is essential to nearly all living organisms. An adult human body contains about 4 grams, mostly in [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]] and myoglobin, which carry and store oxygen, and in enzymes of cellular respiration. Iron deficiency is a common cause of anemia, while excess iron can be toxic.

Agricultural practice of applying controlled amounts of water to land to grow [[Crop|crops]], landscape plants, and lawns. Developed by many cultures, it has been a key aspect of agriculture for over 5,000 years. It sustains crops in dry areas and during below-average rainfall, and is also used to protect plants from frost, suppress weeds, cool livestock, reduce dust, and support mining. [[Drainage]] is often studied alongside it, and both may be needed to sustain high production.

Methods differ in how water reaches plants. Surface (gravity) irrigation is the oldest. Sprinkler irrigation distributes piped water through overhead high-pressure devices. Micro-irrigation delivers water at low pressure through a piped network, and drip irrigation delivers it directly to the root zone. Subirrigation raises the water table to moisten soil below the roots. Water comes from [[Groundwater|groundwater]], from rivers, lakes, or reservoirs, or from sources such as treated wastewater, desalinated water, and fog collection.

Early systems emerged in [[Mesopotamia]], Egypt, the Indus Valley, and China. Irrigated area worldwide grew from 8 million ha in 1800 to 94 million in 1950 and 235 million in 1990. The land equipped for irrigation reached 355 million ha in 2023, up 23% from 289 million ha in 2000, and made up 23% of all croplands. Asia holds 71% of the total. [[India]] (76 million ha) and China (75 million ha) have the largest equipped areas, far ahead of the United States (25 million ha). Irrigated croplands produce 48% of crops by value, and their yield averages 76% higher than that of rainfed land.

Irrigation has environmental costs. Overdrafting depletes underground [[Aquifer|aquifers]], and over-irrigation wastes water and chemicals, may cause water pollution, and can raise water tables, leading to salinity problems that require subsurface drainage.

English polymath: mathematician, physicist, astronomer, alchemist, theologian, historian, and inventor, a key figure in the Scientific Revolution. He was born at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, three months after his father's death.

His book [[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica|*Principia*]] (1687) formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation and established [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]], the dominant scientific viewpoint for centuries until it was superseded by the theory of relativity. With it he derived Kepler's laws of planetary motion and accounted for tides, the trajectories of comets, and the precession of the equinoxes. His work on [[Optics|optics]], collected in *Opticks* (1704), rested on the observation that a prism separates white light into the colors of the visible spectrum; he also built the first reflecting telescope. He shares credit with the German mathematician [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]] for formulating infinitesimal [[Calculus|calculus]], though he developed it years earlier, and he generalized the binomial theorem to any real number. His priority disputes, notably with Robert Hooke over gravitation and with Leibniz over calculus, were bitter.

Newton was a fellow of Trinity College and the second Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the [[University of Cambridge]], appointed at the age of 26. A devout but heterodox Christian, he privately rejected the doctrine of the Trinity and refused to take holy orders in the Church of England. He devoted much time to [[Alchemy|alchemy]] and biblical chronology, but most of that work remained unpublished until long after his death.

Tied politically to the Whigs, he served as Member of Parliament for the University of Cambridge in 1689–1690 and 1701–1702 and was knighted by Queen Anne in 1705. He was Warden (1696–1699) and Master (1699–1727) of the Royal Mint, where he increased the accuracy and security of British coinage, and president of the Royal Society (1703–27). He was the first scientist buried in [[Westminster Abbey]].

Abrahamic monotheistic religion based on the [[Quran]] and the teachings of [[Muhammad]], with an estimated 2 billion adherents, called [[Muslims]]. It is the world's second-largest religious population after Christianity. The Arabic word *islam* means "submission [to God]."

Muslims believe in a primordial faith revealed many times through earlier prophets, including Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, of which Islam is the universal and complete version. They regard the Quran as the verbatim word of God and the final revelation, and Muhammad as the final prophet. His teachings and examples, called the Sunnah, are documented in accounts called hadith. The central doctrine is *tawhid*, the oneness of God, and the creed requires belief in six articles: God, angels, revelation, prophets, the Day of Resurrection, and divine predestination. The righteous are believed to be rewarded in paradise and the unrighteous punished in hell.

The Five Pillars, the obligatory acts of worship, are the creed (*shahada*), daily prayers (*salah*), almsgiving (*zakat*), fasting (*sawm*) in the month of Ramadan, and pilgrimage (*hajj*) to Mecca. Islamic law, [[Sharia|sharia]], touches on virtually every aspect of life. The two main festivals are Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

Islam originated in [[Mecca]] c. 610, when Muslims believe Muhammad received his first revelation. After the move to Medina in 622, Mecca was conquered in 630, and by his death in 632 most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted. Muslim rule then expanded under the Rashidun Caliphate. The two main branches are [[Sunni Islam]] (87–90%) and Shia Islam (10–13%); their division arose from disagreement over the succession to Muhammad and grew to cover theology and law.

Muslims form a majority in 53 countries. About 12% live in [[Indonesia]], the most populous Muslim-majority country, 31% in South Asia, 20% in the Middle East and North Africa, and 15% in sub-Saharan Africa. Pew Research has found Muslims to be the world's fastest-growing major religious group, mainly because of a higher fertility rate and younger age structure.

Period of cultural and scientific flourishing in the history of Islam, dated from the 8th century to the 14th century. It is understood to have begun under the [[Abbasid Caliphate]] during the reign of [[Harun al-Rashid]] (786–809), with the establishment of the [[House of Wisdom]] in [[Baghdad]], then one of the world's largest cities. The institution attracted scholars from across the Muslim world to translate the classical knowledge of the known world into Arabic.

Activity flourished in other centers too, including Cairo, Umayyad Córdoba (capital of [[Al-Andalus]]), Damascus, Samarkand, Kairouan, and Fez. Many works were translated from Greek, Syriac, Middle Persian, and Sanskrit, some later into Hebrew and Latin. Christians, especially of the Church of the East, contributed as translators and physicians. Figures associated with the period include [[Al-Khwarizmi]], whose work laid foundations for algebra; al-Razi, in clinical observation and pharmacology; [[Ibn al-Haytham]], in experimental optics; and [[Averroes]], in philosophy. Suggested causes include Quranic injunctions valuing knowledge, heavy state patronage of scholars, and openness to the learning of conquered civilizations.

The dating is contested. The period is said to have ended with the collapse of the Abbasid caliphate after the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258. Some scholars extend it to c. 1350, to include the Timurid Renaissance, or to the 15th or even 16th century. Others place the true golden age between 750 and 950, arguing that decline began earlier.

The golden-age metaphor was applied in 19th-century writing on Islamic history and became frequent only in the second half of the 20th century. A dominant approach among scholars, the "decline theory," treats the period after the 11th century as an age of decline, a framing that has been challenged. Explanations for the end range from external shocks such as the Mongol sack to internal shifts toward theological orthodoxy, political fragmentation, and changing trade routes.

Piece of land, distinct from a [[Continent|continent]], completely surrounded by water. Islands occur in seas, lakes, and rivers, and no standard of size separates them from continents, which are defined geologically as the largest landmass of a tectonic plate.

Continental islands were split from a continent by [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]]; oceanic islands were never part of one. Oceanic islands form through volcanic activity, grow into atolls from coral reefs, or build up from shoreline sediment as barrier islands. Artificial islands are built by humans, from small outcroppings to large land reclamation projects. Many islands occur in [[Archipelago|archipelagos]]. Chains such as the [[Hawaiian Islands]] are thought to form as plates move over stationary volcanic hotspots, so that islands farther from the hotspot are older and more eroded; the oldest Hawaiian island is 25 million years old, and the youngest, Hawaii, is still volcanically active. Not all chains form this way: the Line Islands are all estimated to be 8 million years old. New Zealand is what remains of a continent that shrank and sank; [[Zealandia]] has had 93% of its original surface area submerged.

Isolation shapes island life. Species reaching oceanic islands evolve in isolation, while continental islands share life with their parent continent but may diverge through natural selection. Islands cover about 6.7% of Earth's land surface yet support roughly 20% of terrestrial biodiversity and around 50% of threatened species. Habitat alteration and invasive species have caused many extinctions, such as that of the dodo on Mauritius.

Up to 10% of the world's population lives on islands. European colonization put the majority of Pacific islands under European control, and decolonization left lasting effects related to industrialization, invasive species, nuclear weapons testing, and tourism. [[Climate change]] threatens islands: sea level rise could submerge the Maldives, the Marshall Islands, and Tuvalu completely, and more intense tropical cyclones damage infrastructure and habitats.
